After alignment

How do we estimate the expression level?

  1. Count reads
  2. Normalization
Counting is the easy half. Deciding what may be counted for a gene is the hard half.

Coverage

The ratio of total number of sequenced/mapped bases against the reference gene/genome

http://www.danielecook.com/calculate-depth-coverage-bam-file/

Coverage

High coverage increases the reliability of sample

Coverage buys confidence about each base. It buys nothing about the biology — that only comes from replicates.

Counting: what may a read be counted for?

Mode A read is counted when
union it overlaps the gene at all — the default, and the most generous
intersection_strict every base of it falls inside one gene
intersection_nonempty the bases that fall in any gene all fall in the same one

A read landing on a place where two genes overlap is ambiguous; one landing outside every gene is no_feature. Both are reported, and neither is counted.

The same BAM and the same GTF give different counts under different modes. The mode is part of the result — write it down.

htseq.readthedocs.io/en/master/htseqcount.html. featureCounts, which the practical uses, has the same choice under different names.

Multi-mapping reads

Not to be confused with multiple sequence alignment. Here one read fits equally well in more than one place in the reference.

Multi-mapping reads

  • Reads are sometimes mapped to multiple locations
  • Keep them, discard them, or split them between the places they fit?
In A. kamchatica the duplicated homeologs are exactly the reads that multi-map. Discarding them would throw away the experiment.

Typical example cases, RNAseq, SNP calling

Normalization RPKM

Expression level is calculated from

  1. Mapped read count coverage depth
  2. Total number of reads
  3. Gene length
Three things drive a raw count, and only one of them is biology. Normalisation is the business of removing the other two.

Normalization

  • Which sample is higher in expression level?
Do not answer yet. The picture is missing the one number that decides it.

Normalization

  • SampleA expression level is twice lower than Control
Twice as many reads, in a library that is five times larger. The ratio is what matters, never the count.

A: 5/50, B: 2/10

Normalization

  • Depends on mapped reads and total reads
Mapped reads and total reads. Neither alone is an expression level.

Normalization

  • Which gene is the most expressed?
Again, do not answer yet. The picture is missing the length of each gene.

Normalization

  • More reads can be mapped on a longer gene
  • Depends on gene length
A long gene collects more reads at the same concentration. Length is the second correction.

Normalization

Corrects for Sums to the same total per sample? Use it for
CPM sequencing depth no counts within one gene, across samples
RPKM / FPKM depth and gene length no historical; still seen everywhere
TPM length then depth yes, 106 comparing samples, and plotting
TMM depth, robust to a few huge genes — what edgeR does to raw counts

FPKM is RPKM counted in fragments rather than reads: for paired-end data one fragment is the two reads together, so it is not counted twice.

None of these belongs in a differential expression test. edgeR and DESeq2 want raw counts and normalise internally.

Mortazavi et al., Nat Methods 5(7):621–628 (2008) · Trapnell et al., Nat Biotechnol 28(5):511–515 (2010) · Wagner, Kin & Lynch, Theory Biosci 131(4):281–285 (2012)

RPKM, TPM

Same data, two scales. Read the axis before you read the plot.

RPKM

RPKM = (Read count × 10⁹) / (Gene length in bp × Total mapped reads)

TPM

  1. RPK = Read count / (Gene length in kb)
  2. Scaling factor = Sum of all RPK / 1,000,000
  3. TPM = RPK / Scaling factor

CPM

CPM = (Read count × 10⁶) / (Total mapped reads)

RPKM divides by total reads. TPM divides by total RPK. That one difference is why only TPM sums to the same number in every sample.

== TCC

  • http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3716788/pdf/1471-2105-14-219.pdf TCC: an R package for comparing tag count data with robust normalization strategies

== RPKM, FPKM

  • RPKM: Reads Per Kilobase of exon per Million mapped reads
  • FPKM: Fragments Per Kilobase of exon per Million mapped fragments
  • Fragment: A set of paired-end reads

Key takeaways: expression quantification

Normalization necessity

  • Three factors affect read counts: Gene length, sequencing depth, expression level
  • Coverage depth: Average number of reads per base position
  • Raw counts are not comparable between genes or samples

RPKM vs TPM vs CPM

  • RPKM: Normalize by length first, then by total reads
  • TPM: Normalize by length first, then scale to 1 million (constant sum)
  • CPM: Normalize only by total reads
  • Key difference: TPM values sum to same total across samples → better for comparison between samples

Practical Guidelines

  • For visualization: Use TPM (comparable across samples)
  • For differential expression: Use raw counts with DESeq2/edgeR (they handle normalization)
  • For coverage analysis: Use CPM or raw depth

A straight line on log-log axes over four orders of magnitude. No linear plot of this data is readable.

Gene Regulatory Network
Scale free network

I guess ....

Gene regulatory networks are generally thought to be made up of a few highly connected nodes (hubs) and many poorly connected nodes. (Wikipedia)
Decourty et al, PNAS 2008
A few hubs and many leaves — the same shape as the expression distribution, and possibly its cause.

Distribution
Count data A. halleri RNAseq

  • Poisson distribution?
Poisson is what you would get if the only randomness were the sampling. It is not.

Distribution
A. halleri FPKM mean - variance

  • Poisson distribution Mean = Variance
    →\longrightarrow Overdispersion Variance > Mean
The variance grows faster than the mean. That is overdispersion, and it is biological, not technical.

Distribution
A. halleri FPKM mean - variance

  • Poisson distribution Mean = Variance
  • Negative binomial distribution
    σ2=μ+ϕμ2(ϕ>0)\sigma^2 = \mu + \phi \mu^2 (\phi > 0)
One extra parameter, φ, and the model fits. Estimating φ well from three replicates is what edgeR and DESeq2 spend their effort on.

Negative binomial distribution

Count the failures k before the r-th success, when each try succeeds with probability p.

It has two parameters where Poisson has one, and the second one is exactly what RNA-seq needs: a variance that is allowed to exceed the mean.

X∼NB(r,p),Pr⁡(X=k)=(k+r−1r−1)(1−p)kprX \sim \mathrm{NB}(r,p), \quad \Pr(X=k) = \binom{k+r-1}{r-1}\,(1-p)^k\,p^r

where rr is the number of successes, kk the number of failures, and pp the probability of success.

Poisson fixes the variance at the mean. Biological replicates never obey that, so edgeR and DESeq2 fit the extra parameter instead of assuming it away.

Figure: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution

Each of these plots answers one question. Decide the question first, then pick the plot.

Box plot
Box-and-Whisker plot

A basic plot 1

A box plot compares distributions. Use it on the samples, before you look at a single gene.

Bar plot

Error bar: standard deviation, standard error, or confidence interval

  • You can see/compare expression levels individually&visually
A bar plot compares a few genes. Always say what the error bar is — SD, SE and CI are three different claims.

Scatter plot for many data points

You can find

  • correlation between samples
  • differential expressed genes visually
  • outlier/strange samples
You are not looking for the diagonal. You are looking for the pair that does not have one.

Scatter plot + Correlation matrix

One number per pair, so a bad sample shows up as a whole bad row.

Heatmap sample - sample

We can see the correlation visually as a quality control, > 5 samples

  • You can see sample correlations visually
  • You can find outlier/strange samples between/within groups
Sample-to-sample first, gene-level second. If two replicates do not correlate, nothing downstream will save them.

Heatmap gene expression - sample

Rows are clustered, so the picture depends on the distance and the linkage you chose. Say which.

Volcano plot log(fold-change) - log(p-value)

X-axis: Log fold change (ratio), Y-axis: -log(p-value)

We can see differential expressed genes visually

Fold change on one axis, significance on the other — because a large change measured badly is not a result.

M-A plot log(average) - log(ratio)

X-axis: Log mean, Y-axis: Log fold change (ratio)

We can see both fold change and expression level at the same time

The MA plot shows the bias a volcano plot hides: whether the fold changes drift with expression level.

Hierarchical clustering

  • You can see sample clusters visually
  • You can find outlier/strange samples between/within groups
Clustering here is quality control, not a result. You are asking whether the replicates believe each other.

PCA: Principal Component Analysis

  • You can see sample clusters visually
  • You can find outlier/strange samples between/within groups
PC1 should be your biggest experimental factor. When it is the batch instead, you have learnt something important.

Heatmap + Clustering

  • You can see gene/sample clusters at the same time
The dendrogram on each edge is part of the figure. A heatmap with clustering is two analyses shown at once.

Multivariate analysis

  • Clustering
  • Multi-dimensional scaling (e.g. PCA)

They are used mostly for quality control after counting

Both of these run before the differential expression, and they are there to catch a mistake, not to find a gene.

Clustering

  • Classify elements with their similarity
Clustering always returns clusters. Whether they mean anything is a separate question.

What is 'Similarity'?

- Distance based:
Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance
- Correlation based:
Pearson correlation coefficient, cosine correlation coefficient
- Link based:
The number of connected nodes, density, (graph theory)
There is no neutral choice of similarity. The metric decides what 'alike' means before any data is read.

Which metric is better?

  • Distance based: Absolute amount of differential expressions
  • Correlation based: Correlation of differential expressions

e.g.

  • Comparison in different conditions →\rightarrow which??
  • Comparison in different time points →\rightarrow which??

Which metric is better?

  • Distance based: Absolute amount of differential expressions
  • Correlation based: Correlation of differential expressions

e.g.

  • Comparison in different conditions →\rightarrow distance based
  • Comparison in different time points →\rightarrow correlation based
Distance asks how much. Correlation asks in what pattern. Time courses want the second; two conditions want the first.

Distance Metrics for RNA-seq Clustering

  • Euclidean: 絶対的な発現量の違いを重視
  • Pearson correlation: 発現パターンの類似性を重視
  • Spearman correlation: ランクベースの相関（ノイズに頑健）
  • 使い分けの指針:
    • 時系列データ → 相関ベース
    • 条件比較 → Euclidean

Clustering

  • Hierarchical Clustering
    • Divisive: top down approach
    • Agglomerative: bottom up approach
  • Non-hierarchical Clustering Partitioning-optimization
    • Hard clustering: elements can belong to only one cluster
    • Soft clustering: elements can belong to more than one cluster
Hierarchical clustering does not need K in advance, and does not give you clusters either — you still cut the tree yourself.

K-means clustering Non-hierarchical clustering

Algorithm

  1. Select K points randomly
  2. Assign clusters to the selected points
  3. Move the centroid in each cluster

Repeat 2-3 until the centroids stop

K-means needs K before it starts, and it will happily return K clusters from data that has none.

K-means clustering Non-hierarchical clustering

Hierarchical clustering

  1. Calculate pair-wise distance in all points
  2. Assign a cluster to smallest distance pair
  3. Select a representative point of the cluster

Repeat 1-3 until the cluster becomes one

Every step merges the two closest clusters and never revisits the decision. An early mistake stays in the tree.

Hierarchical clustering

Distance between clusters

The distance between two points is settled. The distance between two clusters is a choice, and it changes the tree.

Linkage Distance between clusters is Tends to give
Group average the mean over all pairs balanced, middle-of-the-road trees
Nearest neighbour (single) the closest pair long straggling chains
Furthest neighbour (complete) the farthest pair compact, equal-sized clusters
Ward the increase in total variance on merging compact clusters of similar size
The next four slides merge the same points and do not all merge the same pair.

Group average

  • A-C merging

Nearest neighor

  • A-C merging

Furthest neighbor

  • B-C merging

Ward's method, minimum variance

Merge the pair of clusters whose union adds the least to the total spread:

Δ = L(P∪Q) − L(P) − L(Q)

where L(X) is the variance between the centroid W of X and its members.

The other methods ask how far apart two clusters are. Ward asks what joining them would cost.

Ward tends to produce clusters of similar size, which is flattering — and a reason not to read too much into the shape of the tree.

A problem in expression data

  • Expression data are NOT normal distributed
    →\rightarrowHigh and low expressed genes are not evaluated equally
Almost every method you are about to use assumes something close to a normal distribution. Counts are not.

Example

→\rightarrowHigher expressions cause longer distance

Transformation

The problem is the shape of the distribution, so the fix has to change the shape.

  1. Square root — mild; keeps zeros
  2. Log — strong; log2(x + 1) because log 0 is undefined
Transformation
changes the shape of the distribution: it pulls the long right-hand tail in, so that a gene expressed a thousand times over does not decide every distance.
Scaling
moves and stretches the distribution without changing its shape — mean normalisation, Z-score. It makes genes comparable to each other.
Do the transformation first and the scaling second. The other order scales a distribution that is still skewed.

DESeq2 offers two better transformations for small experiments: VST and rlog. edgeR usually works on log2(CPM + 1).

note

(3) rlog transformation (4) VST transformation

  • VST (Variance Stabilizing Transformation): DESeq2での推奨手法
  • rlog transformation: サンプル数が少ない場合に推奨
  • Log2(CPM + 1): EdgeRでよく使用される

Scaling

Another normalization, standardization

Feature scaling is a method used to standardize
the range of independent variables or features
of data. In data processing, it is also known
as data normalization and is generally performed
during the data preprocessing step (wikipedia).
Transformation changes the shape of the distribution. Scaling only moves and stretches it. They are not alternatives.
